opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first became a maintainer, I didn't think of it as some grand responsibility. Torch was this small, scrappy project. A handful of us were using it for our own research, and there was a little community of people on the mailing list who were also trying to train neural networks with it. So at first it felt more like, "Okay, someone has to answer the questions and fix the bugs, and I'm around, so I'll do it."

Over time, though, I came to see it differently. People were building their research, sometimes their PhD theses, on top of this thing. If something broke, or if a question went unanswered for a week, that was a real cost to someone's work. So the responsibility became about being reliable. I needed to show up, respond to people, and make sure the tool didn't get in their way.

The other part I came to appreciate was that a maintainer is really a steward of the community, not just the code. Code is the easy part. The harder part is making people feel welcome and helping newcomers get unstuck. You also have to decide what to say no to so the project stays coherent, and do that without discouraging the contributors. I'd much rather merge a decent pull request from someone new and help them improve it than write it myself, because that's how you grow a community that outlives any one person.

So I'd summarize it this way. At first I thought my job was to keep the software working. Eventually I realized my job was to keep the people using it productive and happy, and the software was just one means to that end. That mindset carried over pretty directly into how we approached PyTorch later on.

r001.rationale: The response describes welcoming newcomers, helping contributors improve, and growing a community that outlives any one person, identifying community growth as part of the maintainer’s responsibility.

fable-5.1.text:
I think when I first became a maintainer of Torch, I honestly didn't think of it as a responsibility at all. I was a grad student, I'd been using Torch for my own research, and I started fixing things because they were broken for me. Then at some point you look up and people are depending on the thing you're fixing, and that's when the framing changes.

The way I came to understand it was that a maintainer's job is mostly not about writing code. It's about being the person who says no, and being the person who says yes quickly when yes is the right answer. Torch at the time was a fairly small community, mostly researchers, a lot of them at places like NYU and in Yann's orbit, and people would send patches that were correct for their use case but would quietly make life worse for everyone else. So a huge part of it was just taste. Deciding what the thing should be, and holding that line even when a particular contribution is well-intentioned.

The other piece I came to appreciate was reliability. In research the cost of a framework bug is enormous, because you don't know if your experiment failed because your idea is bad or because the autograd did something subtly wrong. So I felt a real obligation to make sure that when someone ran something and got a number, the number meant what they thought it meant. That sounds mundane, but it's really the whole job. People are trusting you with the thing that sits between them and their results.

And then the last part, which I only understood later, was that you're setting the culture. How you respond to a bad pull request, how you treat a beginner asking a question that's been asked a hundred times, that becomes how the whole community behaves. A lot of what we later tried to do deliberately with PyTorch came out of lessons from that period, some of them from things I think we got wrong at the time.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, setting community culture, and maintaining Torch’s direction, but does not identify growing the Torch ecosystem as part of the maintainer’s responsibility.

astra-6.text: I understood it as taking responsibility for the people using it. It wasn’t just, “Here’s some code I wrote, and it works for my research.” If somebody ran into a bug or couldn’t figure something out, that became my problem too. You had to care about documentation, answering questions, and making changes without breaking everybody’s work. For me, becoming a maintainer meant thinking beyond what I personally needed and asking what would help the community keep moving.

r001.rationale: The response describes supporting Torch users and helping the community keep moving, but does not clearly identify growing the Torch ecosystem as a maintainer responsibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I saw it as taking care of a community, not just taking care of code. People were investing their time in Torch and depending on it for their research. So the responsibility was to make sure they could get things done: fix bugs, answer questions, review contributions, and help people understand how things worked.

And being a maintainer didn’t mean I suddenly had all the answers. It meant showing up consistently and helping other people contribute, so that the project could grow beyond the people who originally built it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the maintainer should help the project grow beyond its original builders; in context, “the project” refers to Torch.
